episode_title: 373 - Giving Less F_cks About My Clients’ Results Made Me Richer & A Better Coach

real_qa.q: How does giving less responsibility to coaching clients actually increase a coach's income and client results?
real_qa.r: The more responsibility Jill gave back to her clients, the more capacity she had to make more money and sign more people and impact more clients. When she stopped obsessing over their results and created boundaries, the coaching relationship improved because it was no longer contingent on her over-delivering or sacrificing herself to keep clients happy. Her self-sacrifice was not actually serving anybody—by constantly intervening and being endlessly available out of fear clients wouldn't get results, she was actually communicating that her coaching wasn't enough and creating codependence.

real_qa.q: Why do coaches obsess over client results and how does this sabotage their business?
real_qa.r: Coaches obsess over client results because it's about what those results allow them to believe about themselves, not actually about the client. Jill describes being on the moon when a client posts a screenshot of success but questioning herself when they don't—the obsession is rooted in deriving worthiness and identity from client outcomes. This belief that a coach's value depends on every single client getting results holds their confidence and identity hostage to people who should not be holding it hostage.
real_qa.requete: coaches obsess client results sabotage business

real_qa.q: What is the savior complex in coaching and why does it hurt the coach-client relationship?
real_qa.r: The savior complex is the belief that a good coach must care deeply about clients and take responsibility for their results, even when clients aren't doing the work or showing up to calls. Jill used to believe that caring more made her superior to coaches who didn't care as much, but this created codependence because it was rooted in her need to feel worthy and essential. The problem is this belief attracts and reinforces clients who don't take action, because the coach's attitude and energetic frequency is communicating distrust and the need to constantly intervene.

real_qa.q: How should a coach maintain confidence when not all clients get results?
real_qa.r: A coach must hold their power and believe they are phenomenal at their work even when some clients don't get results. Jill explains that you cannot control client outcomes—some clients only benefit from the work months or years after the coaching ends, some have life circumstances intervene, and some realize they don't actually want to do the work. The most successful business owners believe that nothing external can shake their self-concept; they only believe in themselves, not in their clients' outcomes.
real_qa.requete: coach confidence clients don't get results

real_qa.q: How did Jill Parekh's sales messaging change when she stopped tying her self-worth to client results?
real_qa.r: When a client sent Jill a screenshot of success, she sold future offers with total power and conviction. But when the wins channel was quiet for weeks, she couldn't talk about the offer with that same belief because she felt the clients weren't doing well. Once she stopped making her identity contingent on client outcomes, she could sell consistently with power regardless of whether clients were celebrating wins that week, because her confidence was no longer dependent on external validation from client results.
